summary.title: 3D Genome Analysis Identifies Enhancer Hijacking Mechanism for High-Risk Factors in Human T-Lineage Acute Lymphoblastic Leukemia
summary.authors: Lu Yang; Fengling Chen; Haichuan Zhu; Yang Chen; Bingjie Dong; Minglei Shi; Weitao Wang; Qian Jiang; Leping Zhang; Xiaojun Huang; Michael Q Zhang; Hong Wu
summary.executive_summary: This study investigates the role of 3D genome alterations in the pathogenesis and prognosis of T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). By integrating Hi-C and RNA-seq data from 18 newly diagnosed T-ALL patients and 4 healthy controls, the authors demonstrate that 3D genome organization hierarchically classifies T-ALL subtypes according to T cell differentiation trajectories. The analysis reveals that 3D genome alterations are associated with nearly 45% of upregulated genes in T-ALL. A key finding is the identification of 34 previously unrecognized translocations in noncoding regions and 44 new translocation-mediated loops. These structural changes facilitate enhancer hijacking, particularly of the HOXA cluster, leading to ectopic expression of specific transcription factors. The study further dissects the heterogeneity of HOXA-positive T-ALLs, distinguishing between 3'HOXA+ and 5'HOXA+ subgroups based on TAD boundary shifts and enhancer interactions. Clinically, the authors show that ectopic expression of HOXA11-A13, but not other HOXA genes, is associated with immature phenotypes and poor survival outcomes. The findings suggest that 3D genome rewiring, specifically through translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking, drives the specific pathogenic gene expression profiles of T-ALL subgroups. Furthermore, the association of HOXA11-A13 positivity with JAK-STAT pathway mutations and poor prognosis suggests that anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit this high-risk patient group. This work provides a mechanistic framework linking chromatin architecture to oncogene activation and clinical outcomes in T-ALL.

judge_context:
Executive Summary
This study investigates the role of 3D genome alterations in the pathogenesis and prognosis of T-lineage acute lymphoblastic leukemia (T-ALL). By integrating Hi-C and RNA-seq data from 18 newly diagnosed T-ALL patients and 4 healthy controls, the authors demonstrate that 3D genome organization hierarchically classifies T-ALL subtypes according to T cell differentiation trajectories. The analysis reveals that 3D genome alterations are associated with nearly 45% of upregulated genes in T-ALL. A key finding is the identification of 34 previously unrecognized translocations in noncoding regions and 44 new translocation-mediated loops. These structural changes facilitate enhancer hijacking, particularly of the HOXA cluster, leading to ectopic expression of specific transcription factors. The study further dissects the heterogeneity of HOXA-positive T-ALLs, distinguishing between 3'HOXA+ and 5'HOXA+ subgroups based on TAD boundary shifts and enhancer interactions. Clinically, the authors show that ectopic expression of HOXA11-A13, but not other HOXA genes, is associated with immature phenotypes and poor survival outcomes. The findings suggest that 3D genome rewiring, specifically through translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking, drives the specific pathogenic gene expression profiles of T-ALL subgroups. Furthermore, the association of HOXA11-A13 positivity with JAK-STAT pathway mutations and poor prognosis suggests that anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit this high-risk patient group. This work provides a mechanistic framework linking chromatin architecture to oncogene activation and clinical outcomes in T-ALL.

Research Context
Recent studies have demonstrated that 3D genome alterations play important roles in tumorigenesis. However, how such alterations may provide key insights into T-ALL patients is largely unknown. The study aims to integrate 3D genome alterations with differentially expressed genes. Previous work established that 3D genome changes affect hematological malignancies.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The central question is how 3D genome alterations influence T-ALL development and prognosis. The authors hypothesize that 3D genome organization classifies T-ALL subtypes by differentiation stage. They predict that translocations will lead to enhancer hijacking of oncogenic genes. The study tests if ectopic HOXA expression correlates with poor clinical outcomes.

Methodological Details
The study recruited 18 newly diagnosed T-ALL patients and 4 healthy T cell controls. Leukemia blast cells were purified by FACS using specific antibody markers. RNA-seq libraries were prepared using the TruSeq RNA Library Prep Kit v2. Paired-end RNA-seq reads were generated with an average depth of 15 million read pairs. Hi-C was performed on one million cells per sample using the BL-Hi-C protocol. Hi-C raw data were processed using the in-house HiCpipe framework. Compartment analysis used eigenvector command of Juicer under 100 kb resolution. TAD boundaries were calculated by the Insulation score method on pooled 40 kb matrices. Loops were called by HiCCUPS and differential loops adapted from Douglas et al. Translocations were detected using an adapted version of hic_breakfinder. The average depth of patient Hi-C samples was 486 million read pairs. ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data were processed using Bowtie2 and MACS2. DESeq2 was applied to identify differentially expressed genes with FDR <0.01.

Procedures And Architectures
The study utilized a multi-omics approach integrating Hi-C and RNA-seq. 3D genome features included compartments, TADs, and loops. Translocation-mediated loops were manually recorded on interchromosome Hi-C maps. Breakpoints were refined to single base-pair resolution using chimeric reads. Enhancer hijacking was identified by linking translocated enhancers to target genes. The HOXA cluster was analyzed for TAD boundary shifts and enhancer interactions. Clinical outcomes were analyzed in a cohort of T-ALL patients. Multivariate analysis was used to assess independent predictors of survival.

Key Results
3D genome alterations were associated with nearly 45% of the upregulated genes in T-ALL. Approximately 29% of the DEGs were associated with 3D genome alterations. The study identified 34 previously unrecognized translocations in noncoding regions. 44 new loops were formed between translocated chromosomes. Nearly 78% of translocation-mediated loops with CTCF motifs were linked to convergent motifs. ETP ALL samples were arrested at the LMPP to Thy1 stages. Non-ETP samples were arrested at the Thy2 to Thy4 stages. A strong positive correlation (0.685) was found between gene expression and loop strength. HOXA11 or HOXA13 positivity was associated with poor overall and event-free survivals. HOXA13+ status served as an independent predictor for overall survival. HOXA11-A13+ cases were characterized by DN and ETP phenotypes. A higher rate of JAK-STAT pathway gene mutations was observed in HOXA11-A13+ cases.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
3D genome organization represents different frozen stages of T cell development. Translocation-mediated enhancer hijacking drives ectopic transcription factor activation. Different fusion events preferentially alter the 3D genome interactome within the HOXA cluster. The findings highlight the role of 3D genome alterations in T-ALL etiology.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study relies on a small sample size of 18 T-ALL patients. The association of HOXA9 with poor prognosis was not supported in this cohort. The mechanism for diverse HOXA expression patterns by fusion proteins is complex. The study focuses on newly diagnosed patients, limiting generalizability to relapsed cases.

Claims
3D genome alterations are a major driver of gene dysregulation in T-ALL. 3D genome alterations were associated with nearly 45% of upregulated genes. Structural changes at all 3 levels were seen in key transcription factors. Only 29% of all DEGs were associated with 3D genome alterations. 3D genome analysis can serve as a biological readout for functional impact.
Translocations cause enhancer hijacking, leading to specific T-ALL subtypes. 34 novel translocations and 44 new loops were identified. Enhancer hijacking of HOXA cluster was observed.  Translocation-mediated loops may be mediated by loop extrusion.
Ectopic HOXA11-A13 expression is a marker for poor prognosis. HOXA11 or HOXA13 positivity was associated with poor survival. HOXA13+ was an independent predictor for overall survival. HOXA9, a previous biomarker, was not associated with poor outcomes. Anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors may benefit this high-risk group.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The study used multiple levels of 3D genome analysis (compartment, TAD, loop). Differential loop detection was adapted to minimize bias by distance ranges. Translocations were manually assessed to filter false positives.

Ethical Considerations
Samples were collected under the protocol approved by the ethics committee. Healthy donor samples were obtained under ethics committee approval.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows 3D genome and transcriptome clustering of T-ALL subtypes. Figure 2 illustrates the T cell developmental trajectory projection. Figure 3 details translocation-mediated loops and enhancer hijacking. Figure 4 analyzes HOXA cluster TAD boundaries and enhancer interactions. Figure 5 maps breakpoints for HOXA translocation cases. Figure 6 presents clinical outcome associations with HOXA expression.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the identification of 3D genome alterations driving T-ALL heterogeneity. 2. The strongest evidence is the link between HOXA11-A13 expression and poor survival. 3. The future path involves using anti-JAK-STAT inhibitors for high-risk T-ALL.
